But the new bottleneck is not production but supervision: silent regressions, review, and coordination.
The real management job is verification. Here is the exact five-step checklist to run before you ship.
That is not a universal benchmark. It is evidence of what happens when execution becomes cheap enough to run concurrently: output stops being the bottleneck. Supervision becomes the job. OpenAI (https://openai.com/index/how-agents-are-transforming-work/)
The framework below combines a four-part delegation contract with a five-step supervision loop, so agent work stays useful without turning the operator into a human API.
 

Agents turn cheap execution into an expensive coordination problem
This guide is for founders, operators, creators, developers, and knowledge workers delegating real tasks to agents.
 
The task could be code, research, reconciliation, content production, data analysis, customer operations, or internal tooling - the domain changes. The management problem stays recognizable.
Agents reduce the cost of attempting work.
They do not automatically reduce the cost of deciding:
What deserves to be done
Which context is authoritative
What tradeoffs are acceptable
How completion will be verified
Who owns the result after delivery
The shift is already visible in agent usage.
OpenAI describes agents as moving knowledge work from short interactions toward delegated, long-horizon tasks. In its sampled individual-user data for May 2026, 80.6% made at least one Codex request estimated to take more than 30 minutes of human work, and 70.2% made one estimated to take more than an hour. OpenAI explicitly says these model-estimated thresholds should be treated as directional, not exact. OpenAI (https://openai.com/index/how-agents-are-transforming-work/)
Anthropic found a complementary division of labor in its privacy-preserving analysis of roughly 400,000 Claude Code sessions from October 2025 through April 2026. People made about 70% of planning decisions, while Claude made about 80% of execution decisions. Anthropic (https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-code-expertise?level=0)
That is the operating model hiding inside the data:
Human: direction, constraints, judgment.
Agent: search, production, iteration.
Problems begin when nobody defines that boundary.
The operator then becomes the routing layer between agents. They copy context into each task, answer preventable questions, reconcile incompatible outputs, and inspect piles of plausible work.
The agent is active.
The operator is trapped.
Delegation works when intent and evidence travel with the task
The core mechanism is a closed delegation loop.
 
A task leaves the operator with four things attached:
An outcome
A context boundary
Decision rights
Verification evidence
The agent returns an artifact plus proof. The operator reviews exceptions and consequential decisions, not every intermediate action.
Why does this work?
Agents can generate many actions from one instruction. Anthropic observed around 10 Claude actions per user prompt on average in its historical dataset, with some prompts triggering more than 100. A vague instruction can therefore multiply ambiguity before the next checkpoint. A precise instruction multiplies useful execution. Anthropic (https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-code-expertise?level=0)
The same research found that expertise was visible through three behaviors: precise framing, asking for verification. and correcting the agent when necessary. Domain experts also produced longer chains of work per instruction than novices. This is evidence from Claude Code sessions, not proof that every agent workflow behaves identically, but the operating lesson transfers cleanly.
Expertise is not typing every step yourself.
Expertise is encoding the right boundaries before execution begins.
That creates a useful split:
Delegation defines what good looks like.
Execution produces the result.
Verification tests the result against reality.
Escalation returns only unresolved judgment to the operator.
Remove verification, and the system rewards convincing output.
Remove escalation rules and the agent either guesses or interrupts constantly.
Remove decision rights and both human and agent touch every choice.
The goal is not maximum autonomy. It is minimum unnecessary coordination.
A four-part contract makes agent work reviewable
Start each substantial task with a delegation contract.
Do not write a longer prompt merely to sound precise. Write a compact specification that makes the output testable.

Now the agent can move quickly without silently redefining the job.
Run the contract through a lightweight supervision loop:
Dispatch: assign the contract and record the expected artifact.
Checkpoint: inspect early structure only when a wrong direction would be costly.
Verify: run the completion checks against the returned evidence.
Escalate: resolve exceptions, conflicts, and irreversible choices.
Record: preserve the artifact, evidence, and decision for reuse.
A checkpoint is not an invitation to micromanage.
Use it when the path is expensive to reverse: a destructive migration, a public claim, a financial commitment. Or a task with ambiguous source material. Skip it when the work is reversible, and verification is cheap.
The record matters because repeated work should get easier. A corrected criterion becomes part of the next contract. A discovered failure case becomes a permanent check. The operator system improves without requiring the agent to remember an undocumented conversation.
More agents amplify weak boundaries before they amplify output
Parallelism is valuable when tasks are independent, and their outputs share a stable interface.
It is expensive when agents depend on hidden state from one another.
Watch for these failure modes:
The human message bus
Agent A needs information from Agent B, but only the operator can transfer it. Every dependency becomes another copy-paste task.
Fix: use a shared artifact with an explicit owner, schema, and update rule.
The plausible completion
The output looks finished, but no external evidence confirms it.
Fix: require receipts such as passing checks, reconciled totals, source links, diffs, or reproducible commands. Anthropic's strict verified-success measure similarly required a judged success plus at least one hard signal. Anthropic (https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-code-expertise?level=0)
The silent policy decision
An agent encounters ambiguity and chooses a policy instead of escalating it.
Fix: separate reversible implementation choices from decisions involving money, access, publication, compliance, or reputation.
The review avalanche
Five agents finish together. The operator receives five long reports with different structures.
Fix: define one return format and cap the evidence needed for routine cases. Send exceptions to a separate section.
The premature swarm
Several agents explore the same unclear problem before the operator has defined success.
Fix: use one agent to clarify the decision surface first. Parallelize only after the work can be partitioned.
Do not use an agent system when the task takes less time to complete than to specify and verify.
Avoid it when acceptable output depends on tacit taste that you cannot yet express, the action is irreversible, source access is incomplete, or no independent completion check exists. In those cases, use an agent for preparation while keeping execution with the accountable human.
Autonomy should follow observability.
The AI agent design checklist catches failure early
Use this before adding another agent, tool, or workflow.
Name one outcome.
Write the artifact or decision that must exist when the task ends.
2.  Bound the context.
Identify authoritative sources, relevant records, and assumptions the agent must not make.
3. Assign decision rights.
Separate choices the agent can make from choices requiring approval.
4. Define evidence.
Require observable proof for every material completion claim.
5. Create an exception lane.
Tell the agent how to report conflicts, missing access, uncertainty, and failed checks.
6. Standardize the return.
Use one structure for results, evidence, unresolved issues, and recommended next action.
7. Preserve the receipt.
Save the contract, artifact, verification result, and human decision so the next run starts stronger.
You should see: fewer clarification messages, smaller review surfaces, comparable outputs, explicit uncertainty, and failures that appear before consequential action.
If you still need to translate every message, inspect every step, and reconcile every result manually, the problem is not agent capability alone. The work has no stable operating interface.
Cheap execution does not remove management. It makes good management more valuable.
Run the AI agent supervision checklist against one recurring workflow before you add another agent.
